content: In the other thread, we discussed implementation of GraphLike as a class with vertex set and a dart set. I am starting a new thread to discuss what is the best way to implement this instance.

I have made minor modification to @Laura Monk 's work by removing graph-related assumption to create Graph-unaware dart type and implemented GraphLike for Graph using it.

inductive Dart (α β : Type*)
| Dir (e : β) (x y : α) (hne : x ≠ y) : Dart α β
| Fwd (e : β) (x : α) : Dart α β
| Bck (e : β) (x : α) : Dart α β

def Dart.edge (d : Dart α β) : β := match d with
| Dart.Dir e _ _ _ => e
| Dart.Fwd e _ => e
| Dart.Bck e _ => e

def Dart.fst (d : Dart α β) : α := match d with
| Dart.Dir _ x _ _ => x
| Dart.Fwd _ x => x
| Dart.Bck _ x => x

def Dart.snd (d : Dart α β) : α := match d with
| Dart.Dir _ _ y _ => y
| Dart.Fwd _ x => x
| Dart.Bck _ x => x

instance : DartLike α (Dart α β) where
  fst d := d.fst
  snd d := d.snd

instance : GraphLike α (Dart α β) (Graph α β) where
  verts G := V(G)
  darts G := { d | G.IsLink d.edge d.fst d.snd }
  fst_mem_of_darts h := h.left_mem
  snd_mem_of_darts h := h.right_mem
  Adj G := G.Adj
  exists_darts_iff_adj {G u v} := by
    refine ⟨?_, fun ⟨e, he⟩ ↦ ?_⟩
    · rintro ⟨d, ha, rfl, rfl⟩
      exact ha.adj
    obtain rfl | hne := eq_or_ne u v
    · exact ⟨Dart.Fwd e u, he, rfl, rfl⟩
    exact ⟨Dart.Dir e u v hne, he, rfl, rfl⟩

Jun Kwon said:

Can you elaborate more on "half-loops"? What exactly do you mean by that?

When you construct the adjacency matrix of a Graph, for loops, the matrix element is 2 times the number of loops. This is consistent with counting walks indexed by Darts, if you consider each Dart corresponds to 2 distinct orientations on one loop. This is the reason why this choice is so crucial. However some people (I have seen this in articles) allow half-loops, which would be only counted once in the adjacency matrix. In particular, there is only one Dart associated to a half-loop. I do not use this convention so I will not argue for it, and in particular I do not think the current set-up of Graph would allow it naturally, but I think now is a good time to decide.

After a quick Google this does not seem too common a notion so hopefully it is probably acceptable to ignore this, but I am happy to be proven wrong. The current convention is great for the handshaking lemma as well.
Oh, so this is 'Should degree contribution of a loop be 1 or 2?' but on the dart level.

I understand that if anyone imagines that loop should be a single dart, they would probably want a different definition of Dart type. I am also tempted to semi-ignore this possibility. In my opinion, two darts notion is much nicer.

Also, I just realised we might have a bit of a problem with the Dart type def.
If vertices u and v have edge e between them, and we map/take minor of the graph s.t. u and v are mapped to the same vertex w. This turns e into a loop. But how do we decide whether uev should be mapped to fwd e w or veu? Without some total ordering of vertices, it seems difficult to do this.

I ran into the same problem trying to define morphisms. I thought a natural definition for a morphism of Graph should be a map from vertices to vertices and edges to edges preserving IsLink. I would have liked this to induce a morphism at the dart level. However, for the same reason, I was not sure it would work.

@Laura Monk, I agree that the degree of the loop should be 2. But I am wondering if it is fine to have just one dart for a loop. I am trying to imagine a definition of dart that has two loop darts but none of them seems to play well with maps. What is your argument for two loop darts?

I think the degree should be the nb of emanating darts. The adjacency matrix has a weird expression in terms of edges due to the factors of 2 with loops but in terms of darts it is the sum of values at the end of darts starting at the vertex. I imagine darts as the unitary tangent space of the graph, i.e. the set of vertices and direction. If you zoom in near a vertex, for each loop, you do see two directions (this would make more sense if we defined the 1-complex associated to the graph). Finally, I think the inv map should be a involution with no fixed point.
Also, and perhaps most importantly, powers of the adjacency matrix should count walks. This is achieved by defining walks from darts, hence counting two possible steps for each loop.
docs#SimpleGraph.adjMatrix_pow_apply_eq_card_walk
Exactly, but for Graph
More and more I think about multigraph, more I think what I actually want to talk about is 1-complex.

There are 4 possibilities in total depending on our answer to the question: "What should have orientation information".

  1. Nothing. We have one loop dart since vev = vev without orientation. Powers of adj mat. counts walks only for loopless graphs. This removes all friction of going between oriented and not oriented edges as nothing is oriented.
  2. Loops. Nonloop edges does not have any notion whether uev is forward direction or veu is forward. However, loop edges have forward vev and backward vev. Then, whenever nonloop edge become a loop edge, (e.g. minor, vertex identification) we have to somehow make a decision about which should be "forward" and which should be "backward". Internally resolving it by noncomputably choosing the direction will lead to inconsistency problem between related graphs (e.g. one graph maps a dart as forward loop but its subgraph maps the same darts as backward loop). Externally resolving it would mean user has to manually input which direction should take the precedence for each edges that becomes a loop.
  3. All edges in the graph. One way is to noncomputably choose an orientation for each edge. But then, given a walk in G ≤ H, considering the same walk in H requires changing the orientations of each dart as they may not agree, even when loops are not involved. The other way is to have different graphs for all possible orientations. This creates many graphs that are, in undirected perspective, duplicate.
  4. Everything in the type. Graph is redefined to require DartLike α β and simply remember vertexSet and edgeSet. This removes all friction of going between oriented and not oriented edges as everything is oriented. This also removes the compatibility issue of Graph (docs#Graph.Compatible) as each edge comes with an inherent end points.

It feels like we are asking too much of darts to take their direction to be meaningful if the edges are not directed. Scenario 3 would work fine if the direction was data on the edge rather than an imposed derived property; I don't think it can make sense otherwise. What is the use-case that motivates knowing/comparing the direction of a dart (as opposed to comparing darts without knowing their direction (direction being an implementation detail))? (Reading back, looks like I totally missed the point here)
I note that GraphLike doesn't require two darts for a loop, which was deliberately implied by the type-based definition: is this an intentional loosening (or am I just reading it wrong)?

The entire point for me to start thinking about darts is the first place is to count walks on graphs with loops, and I absolutely need the fact that loops are counted twice, so this is non-negotiable on my end (for Friedman's theorem, which is arguably an important result). I don't know that the darts of G need to be uniquely defined, so far I had worked with "a dartset", as I do not think it makes sense to have one that is uniquely defined, or a darted graph to start with (in which case morphisms would be dart morphisms).

In any case for morphisms I presume some people will only care about the vertex information, some about the edges. If I have two edges joining two vertices do I have a morphism that switches them? It depends on conventions, and I think the question of the switching of darts might be the same.

Note that in a lot of cases graphs are defined in a tedious symmetric way wich would actually be lighter if they were defined from a dart. This is not always the case, but a lot of examples would be easily defined as darted graphs (meaning you give a vertex set and darts and the adjacency follows). I was wondering if it would make sense to have such a structure.

the instance for Graph does imply two darts for a loop, so I don't think it would be a problem for the Friedman work if that's defined only over Graph; reading the other defs this does look intentional, so I've probably just missed some conversation

We chatted about the Darts carrying minimal information in GraphLike since it is meant to unify the different notions, e.g. they are unaware of edges. In particular they are unaware of loops.

Firstly, I realise there is a fifth option, which I mentioned briefly:

    i. Do we say unordered type cannot be vertices of a graph?
    ii. Do we say graph with unordered type does not have minor/ vertex indetification/ etc.?

Hi! So, from what I am reading, the actual issue is to have chosen that one way is forward and one backward for loops. For instance, if we contract an edge e going from u to v there is naturally two darts, which we can label (e,u) and (e,v).
In terms of examples, it is often useful to have the darts be explicit. It avoids tedious symmetric definitions for IsLink (IsLink e x y if [condition] or [its symmetric]). For the bouquet or the banana graphs, it is clear what the set of darts should be, for the other examples I have in mind as well; for a contraction also, c.f. above.

I feel like we should be cautious to make sure our graphs are still un-directed in essence, and notably we don't create many copies of the same graph with different orientations. In a sense fixing a specific label of directions for the edges is misleading because it causes the opportunity to compare if two directions are "the same". We really do not need this info, just that there are two.

A suggestion: How about having a notion of half-edges on the graph, and IsLink is defined as a symmetric relation on the half-edges? In this case, each loop corresponds to two half-edges, without having them labelled as + and -. An edge is an unordered pair of half-edges that are linked.

I have been playing with the following definition. Apart from that we are no longer able to use an arbitrary type to label the edges, which can be very useful when they carry some external meaning outside the graph, I am happy with this definition. 

structure Graph (α β : Type*) where
  vertexSet : Set α
  halfEdgeSet : Set β
  inc : halfEdgeSet → α
  inc_mem {a : β} (h : a ∈ halfEdgeSet) : inc ⟨a, h⟩ ∈ vertexSet
  inv : β → β
  inv_invol {a : β} : inv (inv a) = a
  inv_ne {a : β} : inv a ≠ a
  inv_mem {a : β} (h : a ∈ halfEdgeSet) : inv a ∈ halfEdgeSet

Here is a near-minimal definition that uses relation to define Graph. I separate out the last two as candidates for removal:

structure Graph (α β : Type*) where
  vertexSet : Set α
  rel : β → β → Prop
  rel_symm : Std.Symm rel
  attach : {d : β | ∃ d', rel d d'} → α
  attach_mem : range attach ⊆ vertexSet

  rel_irrefl : Std.Irrefl rel
  rel_unique : ∀ ⦃a b c : β⦄, rel a b → rel a c → b = c

  1. Irrefl
    This was flagged by @Laura Monk to be optional. I don't understand what it mathematically represents when an half edge is related to just itself.

  2. unique
    This is very interesting because, as far as I can tell, removing this is to define a Graph as a quotient/vertex identification of some SimpleGraph, not just matchings. If Irrefl condition is kept, Graph can even be defined as extension of SimpleGraph β with a downside that G.Adj is not the adjacency relation on Graph but link between half edges. Simultaneously, the entire SimpleGraph API would be available for use in Graph. I am looking around to find a downside to removing this but maybe there is none.

Example def that extends SimpleGraph:

structure Graph (α β : Type*) extends SimpleGraph β where
  vertexSet : Set α
  attach : SetRel.dom {(a, b) : β × β | Adj a b} → α -- defEq to `SimpleGraph.support G → α`
  attach_mem : range attach ⊆ vertexSet

Hi! I think to start with we should probably have Irrefl. But it is nice to know that it would be quite easy to allow for half-edges if it is ever required. This would mean not allowing each loop to be travelled along in 2 different directions, the half-edges which are attached to themselves can only be followed in one direction.

I like the idea of extending SimpleGraph but I wonder if it is a bit too much fun / far away from intuition. The argument to reuse API is nice, we should see if it works in practice. One thought about the walks: if we obtain Walk from the SimpleGraph on an halfEdgeSet, then the empty walk is actually a one-step walk (because it already specifies a half-edge). We would need to define the empty walk outside of this then. In particular it should exist for any vertex (even if isolated); I don't know if we should allow the junk value Walk x x if x is not a vertex.

Maybe one important test for the definition: what would be a morphism between two graphs G and H? Would that be a pair of maps f₁, f₂ acting on vertices and half-edges respectively, such that:

  • if G.rel d d' then H.rel (f₂ d) (f₂ d')
  • if v = G.attach d then f₁ v = H.attach (f₂ d)
    ?

If we just take walk on SimpleGraph and call it a day, that would not be a good definition of walk on Graph. However, the following seems to work with the def extending SimpleGraph β.

inductive Walk (G : Graph α β) : α → α → Type _
| nil (hx : x ∈ G.vertexSet) : Walk G x x
| cons (a b : β) (hrel : G.Adj a b) (ha : G.attach ⟨a, b, hrel⟩ = x)
  (hb : G.attach ⟨b, a, hrel.symm⟩ = y) (w : Walk G y z) : Walk G x z

For homomorphism, I think that should exactly be the definition! In Lean, it would be:

structure Hom {α β γ δ : Type*} (G : Graph α β) (H : Graph γ δ) where
  fᵥ : α → γ
  fₑ : β → δ
  rel_le : ∀ {a b : β}, G.rel a b → H.rel (fₑ a) (fₑ b)
  attach_comm : ∀ {a b : β} {ha : G.rel a b},
    H.attach ⟨fₑ a, fₑ b, rel_le ha⟩ = fᵥ (G.attach ⟨a, b, ha⟩)

I must admit I have not been following this discussion from the beginning, but I'm wondering if you can elaborate a bit on that last point. My intuition has always been to see a hierarchy DiGraph > Graph > SimpleGraph, both in informal mathematical terms and as a possible design for the formal side, in a similar vein as Group > Ring > Field in the algebraic hierarchy. I also don't have any feeling for this idea that a definition that extends from some other definition is more or less meaningful than a standalone definition.

An undirected graph is not a special case of a directed graph. In many contexts, replacing an undirected edge with two arcs in opposite direction makes situation different. For example, the two directed edges make a cycle and a single undirected edge does not. In all edge modification problems, counting the number of modifications behave differently.
Ah, yes, that makes a lot of sense, thanks!

Yes, the "natural" hierarchy here is in the wrong direction, where DiGraph has superfluous information we don't want to carry to Graph etc. There are also significant differences here:

  • no one considers a ring whilst forgetting the underlying groups

  • in an article you can say "let GGG be a group" and we know exactly what you mean.
    As a contrary,

  • people typically have one kind of graphs they care about and will not care about the other models

  • when you introduce a graph in an article you systematically go on to precise what you mean (simple or multi, directed or not).
    In this sense the situation for graph theory is very different from algebra.

A few other points that came to mind:

  • If you want to write the definition of a ring using no lower structure you will have a horrible list of axioms, and you'll have to reprove a lot of things which are not related to rings but groups. This is why it makes sense to extend. Here the direct definition is neat and meaningful. The only reason SimpleGraph is a possible shortcut is because it happens to have been implemented first.
  • I am concerned about the fact that viewing a Graph as a SimpleGraph creates an unnatural situation where most concepts will have 2 definitions (diameter, degree, walk, ...), most will match but not quite so. This feels like a way to run into troubles, and it also raises a lot of not-so-interesting questions as to the meaning of these new concepts.
    So all it all I think I really like the initial plan to have independant concepts and use GraphLike over them.

Perhaps extending SimpleGraph is not the way to go. You have convinced me. It will probably lead to too much confusion for too few benefits. However, unless I missed something, this is not an argument against removing rel_unique. Is that correct?

After all the discussions above and much thought, these following two points are clear.

  • Graph, as currently defined, does not have enough information on its own to properly define Walk, with 2 darts per loop.
  • Attempts to resolve this by changing the definition of Graph leads to
    - "non-free edge type", which leads to a host of other problems. Or
    - Graph being secretly defined as directed graph.

This forces us to consider the option of Walk requiring more than just Graph in its definition. Here is one solution: Requiring Orientation, a structure containing anitisymm version of IsLink.
Given a graph G, and an orientation of the graph D, each edge creates 2 darts, forward and backward w.r.t D. As far as Walk and Dart is concerned, everything works well similar to the case of redefining Graph to be secretly defined as directed graph. It does mean that, without orientation, you cannot talk about Dart or Walk. We could have a lemma that shows partial orientation, possibly empty, can be extended to full orientation of the graph noncomputably.

This is one possible solution, there could be many. However, I believe that Dart and Walk has to have extra argument on top of Graph.
